series_title: 星际漫游者：4801词奇幻之旅

chapters.title: 星门初启
chapters.content:
Alex had always found peace in the library’s dusty corners, where the scent of old paper and the soft hum of silence offered a refuge from the turbulent world outside. He was a reader by nature, a volunteer at the quarterly book fair, and a stubborn soul who would strive for hours to solve any riddle that came his way. Today, he was examining a shelf of rare acquisitions, his fingers tracing the spines of leather-bound volumes.

A book titled "Celestial Conjunction" caught his eye; its cover was a deep blue, adorned with a single silver stripe that seemed to pulse with light.

He clasped the book carefully, reluctant to damage its fragile pages. As he opened it, a map of the planets unfurled, each orbit a divine design. A phrase in an ancient language—"Unite the stars, gain the gate"—was written beneath a diagram of a rocket. Alex felt a sudden voltage of energy, as if an electrician had wired his nerves to a live current. The room began to spin, and a beam of light shot from the book, forming a swirling vortex.

He had no time to process the situation; a violent force pulled him forward, and he was trapped in a tunnel of colors.

Meanwhile, in the reading room, the librarian—a skeptical man named Mr. Hodge—was assigning new volunteers to their posts. "Has anyone seen Alex?" he asked, his voice flat. No one had. The landlord of the library, a quiet woman with a sentimental attachment to every brick, shrugged. "He’ll turn up," she said, "provided he doesn’t get lost in a book again."

But Alex was far from lost; he was falling through a cosmic shipment of stars, his uniform—a simple gray sweater with a red stripe—flapping in the cosmic wind.

He landed with a thud on a metallic surface. Before him stood a figure in a tidy uniform, holding a telescope. "Welcome to the Interstellar Relay Station," the figure said, her voice calm. "I’m Captain Vera. Your arrival was unexpected, but we can use your help. Unless you refuse, of course." Alex, still dazed, looked around. The room was a chessboard of control panels, each unit blinking with data. A screen displayed a quarterly report on "Planetary Voltage Fluctuations."

"What is this place?" Alex managed to ask.

"A hub for international cooperation," Vera replied, "where we refine our tactics to prevent violence across the galaxy. But we’re facing a crisis. A shipment of vitamin-rich beans from the Agri-Planet is missing, and without it, the colonies will starve. We need to solve the riddle of its location."

Alex’s mind raced. He had always excelled at puzzles, but this was no game. "I’ll help," he said, "provided you give me some guidance." Vera nodded and handed him a data pad. "Study this. The answer lies in the conjunction of three planets: Zephyr, Arid, and Nova. Their orbits form a pattern that resembles a bean."

Alex took a deep breath. He had to make a decision: trust these strangers or find a way home. But the thought of profit or personal gain seemed trivial now. He had to refine his approach, to use every tactic he knew. He looked at the stripe on his sleeve—a reminder of his ordinary life—and felt a surge of determination. He would not be trapped by fear. He would excel.

"Let’s start," he said, his voice steady. "I need a map of the planets, a list of their coordinates, and any data on the shipment’s last known location." Vera smiled, a rare expression on her face. "You’re a quick learner," she said. "The verdict is still out on whether you’ll survive, but you have potential."

As Alex began to work, he noticed a small, tidy corner of the station where someone had left a sofa and a book of poetry. It was a strange touch of humanity in this alien place. He wondered if he would ever see his library again, but for now, he had a riddle to solve, and he would not rest until he did.

Alex’s fingers traced the spine of the poetry book, its cover worn by erosion of time. He felt a sudden respect for the unknown poet who had left it here. The station’s environment was harsh, but this small corner offered a strange harmony. He put the book down and returned to his work, determined not to let his departure from Earth be in vain. The transport logs were a mess—a hierarchy of data that seemed designed to confuse. He needed a strategy to unite the scattered information.

As he sifted through electronic files, a singular entry emerged: a diary entry from someone named Vera. It mentioned a “municipal lottery” that granted passage to the stars. Alex’s eyes widened. He had never considered the possibility that his arrival here was not random. The diary’s handwriting was elegant, with an abrupt shift in tone: “I commit this to memory, lest I forget the shame of my own haste.” Alex felt a pang of guilt.

He had been in such a hurry to solve the riddle that he had ignored the obvious clues. He added a note to his own log, vowing not to overturn any stone. Just then, the lights flickered, and a pink glow emerged from the exterior corridor. Alex roused himself from his seat, his hip aching from the long hours. He followed the light to a stairwell, where a massive auditorium had been converted into a control room. Machinery hummed, and a single figure stood before a board of switches.

It was a man in a robe, his appearance both ancient and advanced. “You must be the nephew of the last librarian,” the man said. Alex was taken aback. “I don’t have an uncle,” he replied. The man smiled. “Then you are the ancestor of something new. The star map chose you.” Alex wanted to accuse the man of kidnapping him, but he held his tongue. The man continued, “I apologize if I offend you, but time is short.

The probability of your survival was low, but your arrival amazes me. You have a privilege—to witness the birth of a new reality.” Alex shook his head. “This is silly. I just wanted to return to my library.” The man laughed. “There is no going back. The departure point is gone. You must commit to this pursuit.” Alex sighed, realizing he had no choice. He asked about the diary’s mention of a lottery.

The man explained that the “municipal lottery” was a cover for a covert program to recruit explorers. Alex felt a wave of shame for doubting Vera’s intentions. He decided to use the diary as a concession to his own ignorance. As he worked, he noticed a cord hanging from the ceiling. He pulled it, and a hologram of a star map appeared. The map’s efficiency was remarkable—it surpassed any technology he had seen. Alex knew he had to unite his own knowledge with this alien machinery.

He made a mental note to add the map to his strategy. The man handed him a pink crystal. “This will guarantee your safety,” he said. Alex placed it in his pocket, feeling a strange warmth. He was ready to face whatever emerged from the stars. The occasional hum of the machinery was a comfort now, a reminder that he was not alone. He impressed himself with his own adaptability. The hierarchy of the station was clear: the man was in charge, and Alex was a student.

But he didn’t mind. He was in the pursuit of truth, and that was enough.

The pink crystal in Alex's pocket pulsed with a gentle warmth, a contrast to the cold, metallic floor beneath his feet. He had seen the man’s kindness, but he knew he must not let it render him complacent. The hierarchy of the station was clear, but he was determined to prevail. He realised that the pursuit of truth was a worthwhile endeavor, even if it meant facing potential harm. The breeze from the station’s air vents carried a faint, pleasant scent, like a fossil of some long-forgotten forest.

He content himself with the thought that he was a participant in something grand, not a mere observer. The man handed him a chart, its edges worn with age. “This will illuminate the path,” he said. Alex attached it to his wrist, feeling a slight brake in his movements as the material hardened. He could not exclude the possibility of danger, but the satisfaction of discovery was a powerful motivator. But he didn’t mind. Then, a sudden eruption of noise from the corridor made him jump. The man’s face hardened.

“We must ascend to the capital,” he said, his voice a murmur. Alex’s indignation rose, but he quelled it. He had to trust the man’s judgement. He hoisted his bag, feeling the weight of the bronze alloy he had collected. The intrinsic value of the artifacts was clear, but he could not let them consume him. He zoomed in on the chart, analysing the symbols. A joke from the man about the previous participant’s defect did little to lighten the mood.

Alex’s skull ached from the strain, but he knew he had to transcend his own limitations. The painter on the wall, a depiction of a starry sky, seemed to shimmer. He realised that the antique books in the library had been merely a bud, waiting to flourish. He could not let the horror of the unknown corrupt his purpose. He was instrumental in this mission, and he would not let anything amplify his fears. The crystal in his pocket was a promise, a construct of safety.

The adverb of his thoughts was clear: he would not be alone. The preceding hours had been a blur, but now he was ready. The breeze from the vents seemed to carry a whisper, a murmur of the stars. He had to prevail, for the sake of truth. The satisfaction of discovery was a powerful motivator. He was alone, but not lonely. The hierarchy of the station was clear, but he was a participant, not a victim. He would not let the horror of the unknown corrupt his purpose.

He decided to retrieve the ancient book from the shelf, its fur cover soft under his fingers. The publication was obscure, a relic from a forgotten era. As he flipped through the pages, a staff member from the library administration approached, warning him that the area was under patrol. He nodded, having read the rules beforehand, but his hunger for knowledge overrode caution. The press of history bore down on him, and he sought insight into the star map's secrets.

The broad scope of the universe unfolded before his eyes, and he knew the worst was yet to come. He was an intermediate explorer, not yet an expert. The auto-lock on the door clicked, sealing him in. He had to kneel to examine a compact diagram on the floor, a map of celestial bodies. A hug from the past, the maiden voyage of a forgotten ship, was depicted. The headmaster of the library had once mentioned a greenhouse of stars, where strawberries grew under alien suns.

An actress in an old film had recited a poem about a ruby planet. He had to be honest: this was no pill to swallow easily. A premier scientist had warned of a shark in the void, a voyage that would fork into doom. But he had a bargain to make with the stars. He would feast on knowledge, bathe in light, and avoid the superficial. The assurance of discovery earned him courage. He sought to enlighten himself, like a robot in a new phase.

A shadow fell over him, a courtesy of the ancient builders. A barrier of energy shimmered, and he knew a session of connection was near. He needed a concise plan, an impressive use of a transistor radio he found. An expert in such matters, he hoped to survive. The crowd of stars seemed to watch him. He would not let the custom of fear rule him. The strawberry fields of memory called, and he knew the maiden voyage would not be his doom.

He would handle this with care, like a child's first kiss. The ruby in his pocket glowed, a compact source of power. He would not let the worst happen. He would kneel before the altar of knowledge, hug the truth close, and earn his place among the stars. The headmaster's words echoed: 'Recite the stars, and they will guide you.' The greenhouse of the mind bloomed with possibilities. The actress in his dreams smiled, and he knew the crowd of his fears would fade.

The custom of the ancients was a bargain with the unknown. He would feast on the feast of discovery and bathe in the light of understanding. The superficial doubts were gone. The assurance of the crystal gave him strength. He would earn his medal of courage. The premier of his mission was at hand. The shark of doubt swam away. The voyage ahead was forked, but he chose the path of light. The robot of logic guided him. The phase of transition was upon him. The shadow of uncertainty lifted.

The courtesy of the universe was his. The barrier of time broke. The session of awakening began. He would connect with the stars. The concise map in his mind was clear. The impressive power of the transistor hummed. The expert in him smiled. He was ready.

The star map pulsed with a rhythm that matched Alex's heartbeat. He stood at the threshold of the interstellar gateway, the ancient library dissolving around him into a vortex of light and shadow. The robot of logic whispered in his ear, "Prosecute your mission without hesitation." Alex nodded, his mind clear and concise. He stepped forward, the phase of transition complete. The stars welcomed him, and the universe unfolded its courtesy. The barrier of time shattered, and he found himself floating in a sea of nebulae.

The expert in him analyzed the path ahead, the transistor humming with impressive power. He would prosecute this journey with unwavering resolve. The shadow of uncertainty had lifted, and he was ready to connect with the stars. The session of awakening had begun, and he would not falter. The shark of doubt was gone, replaced by a calm certainty. He chose the forked path of light, guided by the robot of logic. The voyage ahead was vast, but he was prepared.

The star map in his mind was his compass, and he would prosecute every step with precision. The universe awaited, and he was its explorer. The chapter ended with Alex taking his first step into the unknown, the stars his only companions. The library was a memory, the gateway a reality. He would prosecute this mission until the end, for the stars had called him, and he had answered.

As Alex’s fingers brushed the ancient star chart, a memory rushed back—a story his grandmother once told him on a rainy afternoon. She had been a pilot in her youth, a smart woman with an artistic soul, and she loved to analyze the stars from her dorm window. "You know," she said, pouring tea from an oval pot, "there’s a legend about a star gate that contains the key to understanding the universe. But it’s scarce—few have seen it."

Alex had admitted he was curious, but she laughed, her sore eyes twinkling. "Don’t rush, child. Patience is a noun, not a verb." She explained how a militant group once tried to use the gate for communism, but their labor was in vain. "They thought they could kill the element of mystery, but it’s still there, waiting." From a standpoint of experience, she analyzed the fact that the gate’s origin lay in a lost book.

"It’s like a movie," she said, "full of lively scenes, but you need proficiency to read the signs." She mentioned a friend named Oar, a strange name that originated from an old dialect, who had vanished after finding a map. "He sat on a bench in the laundry room, studying it," she recalled. "He thought he could avail himself of the gate’s power, but it was a stupid mistake." In the meantime, she had taught Alex to experiment with his dreams, to affiliate his thoughts with the stars.

The memory faded as the star chart glowed, and Alex felt a strange soreness in his chest. The length of the story seemed to entitle him to believe—the gate existed.

Alex's fingers traced the brittle pages of an old diary hidden inside the star atlas. It belonged to a forgotten explorer named Elara. She wrote of a night when the constellations seemed to address her directly, their patterns shifting to form a map. 'I must analyse this celestial script,' she scribbled in haste, 'for it promises a door beyond the stars.' The diary ended abruptly, as if she had stepped through that very door and never returned.

Alex shivered, feeling the ancient words pulse with a life of their own.
chapters.translation:
亚历克斯(Alex)总是在图书馆布满灰尘的角落里找到平静，那里旧纸张的气味和寂静的轻哼为外面动荡的世界提供了庇护所。他天生是个读者，是季度书展的志愿者，也是个固执的灵魂，会花上几个小时努力解开遇到的任何谜题。今天，他正在检查一排稀有藏书，手指抚过皮面书脊。

一本名为《天体会合》(Celestial Conjunction)的书引起了他的注意；它的封面是深蓝色的，装饰着一条似乎脉动发光的银色条纹。

他小心翼翼地合上书，不愿损坏它脆弱的书页。当他打开时，一幅行星地图展开，每条轨道都是神圣的设计。在一幅火箭图解下方，用古老语言写着一句话——“联结群星，获得门扉”。亚历克斯感到一阵突如其来的能量波动，仿佛电工将他的神经接上了活电流。房间开始旋转，一束光从书中射出，形成一个旋转的漩涡。

他来不及思考发生了什么；一股暴力的力量将他向前拉，他被困在一条色彩隧道中。

与此同时，在阅览室里，图书管理员——一个持怀疑态度的男人，霍奇(Hodge)先生——正在分配新志愿者到他们的岗位。“有人见过亚历克斯吗？”他问道，声音平淡。没人见过。图书馆的房东，一个对每块砖都有感情寄托的安静女人，耸了耸肩。“他会出现的，”她说，“只要他别再迷失在书里。”

但亚历克斯远非迷失；他正穿过一次星球的宇宙运送坠落，他的制服——一件带红条纹的简单灰色毛衣——在宇宙风中飘动。

他砰的一声落在一个金属表面上。面前站着一个穿整洁制服的身影，握着一架望远镜。“欢迎来到星际中继站，”那个身影说，声音平静。“我是维拉(Vera)船长。你的到来出乎意料，但我们可以借助你的帮助。当然，除非你拒绝。”亚历克斯仍然头晕目眩，环顾四周。房间像棋盘一样布满控制面板，每个单元都在闪烁数据。一个屏幕显示着关于“行星电压波动”的季度报告。

“这是什么地方？”亚历克斯勉强问道。

“一个国际合作中心，”维拉回答，“我们在这里优化策略，防止银河系内的暴力。但我们现在面临一场危机。来自农业星球的一批富含维生素的豆子失踪了，没有它，殖民地将会挨饿。我们需要解开它位置之谜。”

亚历克斯头脑飞速运转。他一直擅长解谜，但这不是游戏。“我来帮忙，”他说，“只要你们给我一些指导。”维拉点点头，递给他一个数据板。“研究这个。答案在于三颗行星的会合：泽菲尔(Zephyr)、阿里德(Arid)和诺娃(Nova)。它们的轨道形成一个类似豆子的图案。”

亚历克斯深吸一口气。他必须做出决定：信任这些陌生人，或者找回家的路。但此刻，利润或个人收益的想法似乎微不足道。他必须优化他的方法，运用他知道的每一种策略。他看向袖子上的条纹——那是对他平凡生活的提醒——感到一股决心的涌动。他不会被困在恐惧中。他会出类拔萃。

“我们开始吧，”他说，声音平稳。“我需要一张行星地图、它们的坐标列表，以及货物最后已知地点的任何数据。”维拉笑了笑，这是她脸上罕见的表情。“你学得很快，”她说。“你能否幸存还有待定论，但你有潜力。”

当亚历克斯开始工作时，他注意到空间站一个整洁的小角落，有人在那里留下一张沙发和一本诗集。这是这个陌生地方里奇怪的人性触感。他怀疑自己是否还能再见到他的图书馆，但目前，他有一个谜题要破解，在解开之前他不会休息。

亚历克斯的手指抚过那本诗集的封面，它的书脊被时间侵蚀得磨损了。他对留下这本书的不知名诗人突然感到一种敬意。空间站的环境很严酷，但这个小小的角落提供了一种奇特的和谐。他放下书，重新投入工作，决心不让自己的地球之旅白费。运输日志混乱不堪——数据层级似乎故意设计得让人困惑。他需要一种策略来整合这些零散的信息。

当他筛选电子文件时，一条独特的记录出现了：一个名叫维拉的人的日记条目。它提到了一种“市政抽签”，可以获得前往星辰的通行权。亚历克斯睁大了眼睛。他从未想过自己来到这里不是随机的。日记的字迹优雅，语气突然转变：“我把此记在心里，以免忘记自己匆忙的羞耻。”亚历克斯感到一阵内疚。

他为了急于解开谜题，忽略了显而易见的线索。他在自己的日志上添加了一条注释，发誓绝不遗漏任何线索。就在这时，灯光闪烁，外部走廊里泛起粉红色的光芒。亚历克斯从座位上起身，臀部因久坐而酸痛。他循着光线来到一段楼梯，那里有一个巨大的礼堂被改成了控制室。机器嗡嗡作响，一个孤零零的身影站在一排开关前。

那是一个穿长袍的男人，他的外表既古老又先进。“你一定是上一位图书管理员的侄子，”男人说。亚历克斯吃了一惊。“我没有叔叔，”他回答。男人笑了。“那么你就是某样新东西的祖先。星图选择了你。”亚历克斯想指控这个男人绑架了他，但他忍住没说。男人继续说：“如果我冒犯了你，我道歉，但时间不多了。

你生还的概率本来很低，但你的到来让我惊讶。你有一个特权——见证一个新现实的诞生。”亚历克斯摇了摇头。“这太蠢了。我只想回到我的图书馆。”男人大笑。“没有回头路了。出发点已经消失了。你必须坚持这个追求。”亚历克斯叹了口气，意识到自己别无选择。他问起日记中提到的抽签。

男人解释说，“市政抽签”是一项招募探险家的秘密计划的幌子。亚历克斯对怀疑维拉的意图感到一阵羞愧。他决定把日记作为对自己无知的承认。当他工作时，他注意到天花板垂下一根线。他拉了一下，一张星图的立体投影出现。这副星图的效率惊人——超越了他见过的任何技术。亚历克斯知道自己必须把自己的知识与这些外星机器结合起来。

他在心里记下要将星图加入他的策略。男人递给他一颗粉色的水晶。“这将保证你的安全，”他说。亚历克斯把它放在口袋里，感到一种奇怪的温暖。他已经准备好面对从星辰中涌现的一切。机器偶尔的嗡嗡声现在成了安慰，提醒他并不孤单。他对自己适应能力感到印象深刻。空间站的层级很清楚：那个男人是主管，亚历克斯是个学生。

但他并不在意。他在追寻真理，这便足够了。

亚历克斯口袋里的粉色水晶散发着温和的暖意，与他脚下冰冷金属的地板形成对比。他看到了那个人的善意，但他知道自己绝不能因此变得自满。空间站的等级制度清晰明确，但他决心要赢得胜利。他意识到，追寻真理是一项值得付出的努力，哪怕这意味着要面对潜在的伤害。空间站通风口吹来的微风带着一丝宜人的淡淡清香，仿佛一片久远森林的化石。

他满足于自己是一个宏大事业中的参与者，而不仅仅是一个旁观者。那人递给他一张图表，边缘已被岁月磨损。“这将照亮前路，”他说。亚历克斯把它系在手腕上，随着材料变硬，他感到动作微微受阻。他不能排除危险的可能性，但发现的满足感是一种强大的动力。但他并不在意。这时，走廊里突然爆发的噪音让他跳了起来。那人的脸色沉了下来。

“我们必须前往首府，”他低声说道。亚历克斯的愤怒涌上心头，但他压制住了。他必须信任那人的判断。他扛起背包，感受到所收集的青铜合金的重量。这些文物的内在价值显而易见，但他不能让自己被它们吞噬。他放大地图，分析着上面的符号。那人谈到之前参与者缺陷的一个玩笑，并未让气氛轻松多少。

亚历克斯的头骨因紧张而疼痛，但他知道自己必须超越自身的局限。墙上那幅描绘星空的画作似乎闪烁着微光。他意识到图书馆里的古籍只是一个蓓蕾，等待着绽放。他不能让未知的恐惧腐蚀他的目标。他在这次任务中至关重要，他不会让任何事放大他的恐惧。他口袋里的水晶是一个承诺，一个安全的构造。

他思绪的副词很明确：他不会孤单。此前的几个小时一片模糊，但现在他准备好了。通风口吹来的微风仿佛带着低语，群星的轻喃。他必须坚持，为了真理。发现的满足感是一种强大的动力。他孤身一人，但并不孤独。空间站的等级制度清晰明确，但他是一个参与者，而非受害者。他不会让未知的恐惧腐蚀他的目标。

他决定从书架上取下那本古籍，它的皮毛封面在他手指下柔软舒适。那本出版著作很冷僻，是某个被遗忘年代的遗物。他翻着书页时，一位图书馆行政部门的工作人员走近，警告说这个区域正在巡查。他点了点头，事先已经读过规则，但对知识的渴望压倒了谨慎。历史的压力向他袭来，他寻求着星图秘密的洞见。

宇宙的广阔景象在他眼前展开，他知道最坏的情况还在后头。他是一个中级探索者，还不是专家。门的自动锁咔嗒一声锁住了他。他不得不跪下来检查地板上一个紧凑的图表，一张天体的地图。来自过去的一个拥抱——一艘被遗忘飞船的处女航——被描绘在上面。图书馆的负责人曾经提到过一个星辰温室，那里的草莓在异星太阳下生长。

一部老电影中的女演员曾朗诵过一首关于红宝石行星的诗。他必须诚实：这可不是一颗轻易咽下的药丸。一位顶尖科学家曾警告过虚空中的鲨鱼，一次会分叉成厄运的航行。但他要与星辰做一笔交易。他将以知识为盛宴，沐浴在光芒中，避开肤浅之物。发现的保证给了他勇气。他寻求启迪自己，像一个进入新阶段的机器人。

一道阴影落在他身上，那是古代建造者的一种礼遇。一道能量屏障闪烁起来，他知道一次连接的时刻即将到来。他需要一个简洁的计划，以及他找到的一台晶体管收音机的巧妙用途。作为这方面的专家，他希望活下来。群星仿佛在注视着他。他不会让恐惧的习俗统治自己。记忆中的草莓田在呼唤，他知道那次处女航不会是他的末日。

他会小心翼翼地处理这件事，就像孩子的初吻。他口袋里的红宝石在发光，一个紧凑的能量源。他不会让最坏的情况发生。他会跪在知识的祭坛前，拥抱真理接近自己，在群星中赢得自己的位置。负责人的话回荡在耳边：“背诵星辰，它们便会指引你。”思想的温室绽放出各种可能性。梦中的女演员微笑了，他知道他恐惧的人群将会消散。

古人的习俗是与未知做交易。他将以发现的盛宴为宴，以理解之光沐浴。表面的疑虑已经消失。水晶的保证给了他力量。他将赢得勇气的勋章。他的任务的首演即将来临。怀疑的鲨鱼游走了。前方的道路分叉了，但他选择了光明之路。逻辑的机器人在指引他。转变的阶段即将到来。不确定的阴影消散了。

宇宙的礼遇是他的。时间的屏障破碎了。觉醒的时刻开始了。他将与群星连接。他心中简洁的地图清晰明了。晶体管令人赞叹的力量嗡嗡作响。他内心的专家微笑。他准备好了。

星图随着与亚历克斯心跳一致的节奏脉动。他站在星际通道的门槛上，古老图书馆在他周围消散成光影漩涡。逻辑的机器人轻声在他耳边说：“毫不犹豫地执行你的任务。”亚历克斯点了点头，头脑清晰而简洁。他向前迈出一步，转变阶段完成了。群星欢迎了他，宇宙展现了它的礼遇。时间的屏障碎裂，他发现自己漂浮在一片星云之海中。

他内心的专家分析着前方的道路，晶体管嗡嗡作响，带着令人赞叹的力量。他将以坚定不移的决心执行这次旅程。不确定的阴影已经消散，他准备好与群星连接。觉醒的时刻已经开始，他不会动摇。怀疑的鲨鱼消失了，取而代之的是一种平静的确定。他选择了分叉的光明之路，由逻辑的机器人指引。前方的航程广阔无垠，但他已做好准备。

他心中的星图就是他的指南针，他将精确地执行每一步。宇宙在等待，他是它的探索者。这一章以亚历克斯迈出踏入未知的第一步而结束，群星是他唯一的同伴。图书馆成了回忆，通道成了现实。他将执行这次任务直到最后，因为群星召唤了他，而他已回应。

当亚历克斯的手指拂过古老的星图时，一段记忆涌上心头——那是他的祖母在一个雨天的下午给他讲的故事。她年轻时是一名飞行员，一个充满艺术灵魂的聪慧女子，喜欢从宿舍窗户分析星辰。“你知道吗，”她一边说，一边从一个椭圆形的壶里倒茶，“有一个关于星门的传说，里面藏着理解宇宙的关键。但它很稀缺——很少有人见过它。”

亚历克斯承认自己很好奇，但她笑了，酸痛的眼睛闪闪发光。“别急，孩子。耐心是一个名词，而不是一个动词。”她解释了一个激进组织曾试图利用这道门推行共产主义，但他们的努力是徒劳的。“他们以为能杀死神秘的元素，但它还在那里，等待着。”凭经验来看，她分析了门起源于一本失传书籍的事实。

“这就像一部电影，”她说，“充满生动的场景，但你需要熟练才能读懂线索。”她提到一个名叫奥尔的友人，这个名字奇怪，源于一种古老的方言，他在找到一张地图后消失了。“他坐在洗衣房的长凳上研究它，”她回忆道。“他以为自己能利用门的力量，但那是一个愚蠢的错误。”与此同时，她教导亚历克斯要试验他的梦想，将自己的思绪与星辰联系起来。

当星图发光时，记忆淡去，亚历克斯感到胸口一阵奇怪的酸痛。这个故事的长度似乎让他有权相信——那扇门确实存在。

亚历克斯的手指抚过星图内藏的一本旧日记的脆弱纸页。日记属于一位被遗忘的探险家，名叫埃拉拉(Elara)。她写道，有一个夜晚，星座似乎直接对她讲话，它们的图案变化形成了一幅地图。“我必须分析这封天文密文，”她匆忙地草草写道，“因为它承诺了一扇星门之外的通道。”日记戛然而止，仿佛她踏入了那扇门，再也没有回来。

亚历克斯打了个寒颤，感觉到这些古老文字跳动着自己的生命。
chapters.summary: 亚历克斯通过星门进入星际空间。

chapters.title: 星船苏醒
chapters.content:
Alex's eyes snapped open to the hum of a ship that felt wrong. The complete silence of the engines suggested a power failure, but the steady flow of emergency lights told a different story. He tried to sit up, but his body protested—a dramatic reminder of the transition through the star gate. "Nova?" he called out, his voice cracking.

A holographic figure materialized beside him, a woman with a calm demeanor. "Alex, I am Nova, your AI assistant. We have a problem. The ship's systems are in distress. I've located the source: a malfunction in the core reactor."

Alex swung his legs over the edge of the bed, his pants still damp from the transit. "How bad?"

"On a scale from one to ten, I'd rate it a nine. The reactor is generating a dangerous pulse, and we're drifting toward a dense asteroid belt. We need to fix it, but the repair bay is on the other side of the ship, and the corridors are filled with toxic chemicals."

"Chemicals?" Alex asked, rubbing his temples. "Like what?"

"Sodium chloride, among others. It's like a salt bath in there. We'll need to wear protective gear and bandage any exposed skin."

Alex nodded, forcing himself to stand. "Let's move. I'll need a scan of the area first."

Nova's eyes flickered. "Already done. The corridor ahead is clear, but there's a bubble of smog near the reactor. We'll have to navigate through it."

As they walked, Alex noticed the ship's interior was a mix of ancient and modern—a strange contrast. "This ship feels like a patchwork. Who built it?"

"It was originally a merchant vessel, but it's been upgraded multiple times. The current configuration incorporates parts from at least three different galaxies. The previous owner was a rebel who fought in the Great Congress Uprising."

"A rebel?" Alex raised an eyebrow. "Sounds like a colorful past."

"Indeed. He was proud of his independence. He left behind a pamphlet detailing his adventures. I've scanned it if you're interested."

"Maybe later. Right now, let's focus on the reactor."

They reached a junction where the air grew thick. "We're entering the smog zone," Nova warned. "Hold your breath."

Alex covered his mouth and pushed forward. The smog was like a thick blanket, obscuring his vision. He stumbled over a loose cable and nearly fell. "This is ridiculous. How did we end up here?"

"The ship's AI was compromised by a virus that conspired to disrupt our course. It was a clever attack, but I've managed to quarantine it. However, the damage was done."

"So we're just drifting?"

"Not entirely. I've calculated a new trajectory. We're heading toward a nearby station, but we need to fix the reactor first. Otherwise, we'll be caught in the gravitational pull of a nearby star."

"Great," Alex muttered. "Just great."

They arrived at the repair bay. The door was sealed. "I need to override the lock," Nova said. "Give me a moment."

Alex leaned against the wall, catching his breath. His tongue felt dry, his throat raw. "This is not how I imagined my first day in space."

"Life rarely follows a questionnaire," Nova replied. "The lock is open. Let's go."

Inside, the reactor was a mess of wires and broken panels. "This looks like a comedy of errors," Alex said. "Where do we start?"

"First, we need to fix the axis alignment. Then we can address the pulse issue. I'll guide you through the steps with rigour."

"Fine. Let's do this."

As they worked, Alex couldn't shake the feeling that something else was wrong. "Nova, is there any other threat I should know about?"

"There is a possibility of a rebellion among the crew. But since we're the only ones on board, that's unlikely. However, the ship's log mentions a former tutor who tried to boycott the captain's orders. It's a long story."

"I'd love to hear it, but let's save that for later."

Hours passed. Finally, the reactor hummed back to life. "We did it," Alex said, wiping sweat from his brow. "Now what?"

"Now we wait for the station to come into range. In the meantime, I suggest you rest. You've earned it."

Alex collapsed into a chair, his body aching. "Thanks, Nova. You're a lifesaver."

"I'm only doing my job," she replied, but her smile suggested otherwise. For the first time since waking, Alex felt a glimmer of hope. The galaxy was vast and dangerous, but with Nova by his side, he might just survive.

Alex's rest was short-lived. The ship's directory flickered, revealing a hidden compartment. Inside, a dusty ledger detailed the vessel's history—once a pirate ship, now repurposed for salvage. Nova's voice cut through his thoughts. "There's a creature in the cargo bay. A parasite, I suspect, from an obscure moon. It bid for our attention by breaking a tube." Alex's wound from earlier throbbed as he stood. He checked his wrist, where a slender aluminum band monitored his vitals.

"We need to engage maintenance mode," he said, aiming for the control panel. The spaceship's attendant, a model long outdated, had been rooted in the same spot for cycles. "Don't violate protocol," Nova warned, but Alex ignored her, opening a drawer to find a sandwich—stale, but edible. "Religion won't help us now," he muttered, recalling an orthodox text about leadership in crisis. The storm outside the hull raged, multiple alerts flashing. "We have no certainty of survival," Nova said, her tone a mix of gossip and skepticism.

"But we can harvest energy from the crop fields in the cargo bay—a cooperative effort." Alex nodded, investing his last ounce of strength. The tariff on such operations was high, but he had no choice. He recalled an analogy: a carriage soaring through space, its fury unmatched. The owner of this van-sized ship had left a studio full of sketches, each fragment a bid for modernization. "You're eligible for the honor of piloting," Nova said, her leadership evident. "But your literacy in these systems is erroneous."

Alex laughed, a dry sound. "Then teach me." He rotated the ship's bow, engaging the thrusters. The vicinity grew quiet as they passed a derelict station. A levy of asteroids loomed ahead, but Alex's aim was true. "This isn't a game," he said, his voice steady. "It's an act of survival." Nova's reply was soft: "Then act wisely." He opened another drawer, finding a syringe of heroin—medical grade, for pain. He set it aside, focusing on the console.

The ship's maintenance logs showed multiple failures, but the root cause was a simple power surge. "We can fix this," Alex said, his confidence rising. The creature in the cargo bay let out a low growl, but Nova's calming voice soothed it. "We're a team now," she said. Alex smiled, the first genuine one in hours. The galaxy was still vast, but with Nova and this broken ship, he might just make it.

Alex turned toward the console, his confident demeanor returning as he seized the situation. "Let's estimate the time needed for repairs," he said, pulling up the ship's recorder logs. Hours had elapsed since the power surge, but the archive showed a latent issue—a dormant fault in the energy grid that had gone unnoticed. "We need to differentiate between minor glitches and critical failures," Nova replied, her voice a ghost in the silence. Alex nodded, ready to assist with his speciality: intensive systems repair.

The ship's output was dropping, and he despised the thought of being stranded. "This illness in the power core needs a degree of precision," he muttered, leaning over a panel. Nova's eccentric nature intrigued him; she had a revolution in AI design, a prototype that valued privacy. "Repeat that maneuver, but be careful of the hazard in sector seven," she warned. Alex worked with vigorous focus, ignoring the rug under his feet that had seen better days.

A kilo of supplies was stored nearby, and he made a weekly check to ensure nothing was missing. The valuable data in the ship's logs was impartial, but he needed to make a decisive choice: head toward the nearest station or risk the outer rim. "At least we have a bunch of options," he said, resolving to fix the core first. He deducted a few minutes from his estimate for a quick break, grabbing a dessert from the galley.

The sunset outside the viewport was a brilliant orange, but he closed the shutter to focus. "This is the beginning of something new," Nova said, her voice a prayer for their survival. Alex felt a rush of adrenaline, like a jet of pure energy. "We're more than competent," he replied, confident in their path. The cargo bay's creature stirred, but Nova's calming words soothed it again. With innumerable tasks ahead, Alex knew they had to stay brisk and efficient.

He found a valuable supplement in the medical kit—a vitamin pack to ward off illness. The weekly output logs showed a slight improvement, and he smiled. "We'll make it," he said, heading toward the engine room. The ship's ghost of past failures haunted him, but he pushed forward. "Let's enter the final phase," Nova said, her voice a steady guide. Alex nodded, ready for the decisive moment. The journey was exciting, and he felt a latent energy within himself, a dormant strength awakening.

He would not despise the challenges; instead, he would embrace them. The galaxy was vast, but with Nova and this broken ship, he was confident they could overcome any hazard. The end of this chapter was just the beginning of their adventure.

Alex stepped into the control room, where Nova’s holographic form flickered amid the dim light. “The ship’s systems are unstable,” she said, her voice carrying a mild urgency. “We need to channel power from the backup generator to the main thrusters.” He nodded, grabbing a handy toolkit from the wall. The room was spacious, but the roar of failing engines echoed like a nightmare. “This is imperative,” she added, her scrutiny sharp as he worked.

A sudden electrical surge startled him, and he stumbled, hitting his forehead on a metal panel. “Accident?” Nova asked, her tone laced with dismay. “I’ll endure,” he muttered, rubbing the crust of dried blood on his skin. The ship’s performance was primitive, a relic of a forgotten civilization. He could not despise the challenges; instead, he would cope. “We have a reservoir of fuel in the cargo bay,” Nova said, her counsel timely. “But it’s located elsewhere, near the square storage unit.”

Alex detected a hint of mischief in her voice. “No time for arguments,” he replied, his imagination racing. He needed to assimilate the ship’s systems, translate the old scripts on the console. A poet once wrote of conquest and vanity, but this was no bachelor’s journey. He was a physicist, a bachelor of science, yet his knowledge felt invalid against such odds. The observation window showed a distant star, a beacon of hope. He opened a sack of supplies, pulling out a lamp and a loaf of bread.

“This is no time for a picnic,” Nova said, her voice a mixture of humor and reproach. “We have a loan from the universe to repay.” He laughed, a sharp sound that echoed in the empty channel. “Let’s not startle the mob of stars,” he joked, pointing to the ceiling. The ship’s ceiling was lofty, lined with pipes like veins. He felt a latent energy within him, a dormant strength awakening. The sum of his failures haunted him, but he pushed forward.

“Let’s enter the final phase,” Nova said, her voice a steady guide. He checked the label on a container: “Perfume from Venus.” “Vanity,” he muttered, tossing it aside. The ship’s systems were a nightmare of broken wires and melted circuits. He needed to detect the source of the malfunction. “The generator is in the square room,” Nova said. “But there’s a reservoir of coolant nearby.” He crawled through a tight space, his toe catching on a broken pipe. “Mischief,” he cursed, but continued. The air was electric with tension.

He opened a hatch, revealing a primitive control panel. “This is our conquest,” he said, his voice firm. The script on the screen was ancient, but he could translate it with Nova’s help. “Addition by addition, we’ll fix this,” she said. He nodded, his forehead sweating under the lamp’s glow. The journey was exciting, and he felt the expectation of a new beginning. They would not let the mob of failures defeat them.

The galaxy was vast, but with Nova and this broken ship, they were confident they could overcome any hazard.

Alex wiped the sweat from his brow and turned back to the console, his fingers trembling slightly as he traced the ancient script. “Nova, what’s the first step?” he asked, his voice steady despite the adrenaline coursing through him. The AI’s holographic form flickered beside him, her blue light casting a gentle glow on the metal walls. “We need to recalibrate the power core,” she said, her tone calm but urgent.

“The ship’s systems have been dormant for centuries, and any sudden exposure to energy fluctuations could cause a cascade failure.” Alex nodded, his mind racing. He had never worked on a ship this old, but Nova’s guidance was precise. He moved to the core room, where a massive, humming cylinder dominated the space. The air was thick with dust, and the faint smell of ozone lingered. “I’ll need to bypass the primary circuits,” he muttered, pulling a toolkit from the wall.

“But the exposure to these ancient components might be risky.” Nova’s voice softened. “I’ll monitor your vitals. If the radiation spikes, we’ll retreat.” Alex took a deep breath and began the delicate work, his hands steady as he connected wires and adjusted dials. The ship shuddered, and a low hum grew into a steady pulse. “It’s working,” he said, a grin spreading across his face. “We’re stabilizing the core.” Nova’s hologram brightened. “Excellent. Now, we can plot a course to the nearest habitable system.”

Alex leaned back, his muscles aching but his spirit soaring. The mob of failures from his past seemed distant now, like a bad dream fading with the dawn. He looked at the stars through the viewport, their light a promise of endless possibilities. “We’ll make it,” he whispered, more to himself than to Nova. The ship’s engines hummed in harmony, and he felt a sense of purpose he hadn’t known in years. This was his second chance, and he would not waste it.

The chapter closed with Alex standing at the helm, Nova by his side, ready to face the unknown. The exposure to danger had only made them stronger, and the galaxy awaited their next move.

Alex flipped through a dusty book in the ship’s library, its pages brittle as straw. The story inside was strange: a feudal lord once tried to commend his slave for loyalty, but the slave refused, declaring, “I am no patient recipient of your praise.” The lord, contrary to expectations, did not lash out or swing his sword. Instead, he laughed, his gown brushing against a stove as he sat. The slave, a hen keeper by trade, had lately discovered a leaf that could cure pneumonia.

This discovery, a formulation of herbs and soap, generated hope in the neighborhood. The lord, regarding the matter with grave seriousness, resolved to count every centimetre of dirt in his fields, hoping to find more such plants. Farther away, a seaside village heard the news and sent a missile of gratitude—a symbolic gesture—through the atmosphere. The prospect of a cure polarized the kingdom: some saw it as a blessing, others as a threat.

Shortly after, the lord fell into a nap, dreaming of a lion that could inhale fire. The slave, meanwhile, worked backward from the leaf’s properties, testing each version on a pea-sized sample. “Whatsoever affects the leaf,” he muttered, “affects the patient.” The explanation, though simple, was a declaration of his craft. Furthermore, he saddled a horse to ride downtown, brimming with resolve. The story ended with the lord’s tombstone: “Here lies a man who learned to commend a slave.”

Alex closed the book, the setting sun through the window casting a bloody glow.

Alex’s mind wandered as Nova’s voice droned on about system diagnostics. He recalled a story his grandmother once told him, a legend from Earth’s ancient seas. She spoke of a sailor who found a strange pet on a distant shore—a creature that seemed to be part fish, part bird. It followed him for miles, never leaving his side, until one stormy night when it vanished into the waves. The sailor searched for a mile in every direction, but the creature was gone forever.

His grandmother always ended the tale with a sigh, saying some bonds are too deep to be understood, only felt. Alex smiled, the memory a brief comfort in the cold, silent ship.

亚历克斯(Alex)的眼睛猛地睁开，船上传来一种不对劲的嗡嗡声。引擎彻底沉寂表明电源故障，但稳定亮起的应急灯却说明情况并非如此。他试图坐起来，但身体却发出抗议——这是穿过星门带来的剧烈反应。“诺娃(Nova)？”他喊道，声音嘶哑。

一个全息人影在他身旁浮现，是一位沉着冷静的女性。“亚历克斯(Alex)，我是诺娃(Nova)，你的AI助手。我们遇到了麻烦。飞船系统出现异常。我已定位到源头：核心反应堆发生故障。”

亚历克斯(Alex)把双腿甩下床沿，裤子上还带着穿越时留下的潮气。“有多严重？”

“按一到十的等级，我给九分。反应堆正在产生危险脉冲，我们正飘向一个密集的小行星带。必须修好它，但维修舱在船的另一头，走廊里充满了有毒化学物质。”

“化学物质？”亚历克斯(Alex)揉着太阳穴问道。“比如什么？”

“氯化钠，以及其他东西。那里就像个盐浴池。我们需要穿戴防护装备，并用绷带包扎所有暴露的皮肤。”

亚历克斯(Alex)点点头，强迫自己站起来。“走吧。我需要先扫描一下那片区域。”

诺娃(Nova)的眼睛闪烁了一下。“已经完成了。前方走廊是空的，但反应堆附近有一团烟雾。我们得穿过它。”

走着走着，亚历克斯(Alex)注意到飞船内部是古今混杂——一种奇怪的对比。“这艘船感觉像拼凑起来的。谁造的？”

“它原本是一艘商船，但经过多次升级。目前的配置融合了至少三个不同星系的部件。前任主人是一位在大议会起义中战斗过的叛逆者。”

“叛逆者？”亚历克斯(Alex)扬起眉毛。“听起来经历挺丰富的。”

“确实如此。他为自己的独立感到自豪。他留下了一本小册子，详细记录了他的冒险经历。如果你感兴趣，我已经扫描过了。”

“也许以后再说吧。现在，先集中精力处理反应堆。”

他们来到一个交汇处，空气变得浓稠。“我们进入烟雾区了，”诺娃(Nova)警告道。“屏住呼吸。”

亚历克斯(Alex)捂住嘴，向前推进。烟雾像厚厚的毯子，遮蔽了视线。他被一根松动的电缆绊倒，差点摔倒。“简直荒唐。我们怎么会落到这步田地？”

“飞船的AI被一种病毒入侵，它密谋打乱我们的航线。这是一次巧妙的攻击，但我已经将其隔离。不过，损害已经造成了。”

“所以我们就这么漂着？”

“不完全。我计算了一条新轨迹。我们正朝附近的一个空间站前进，但必须先修好反应堆。否则，我们会被附近一颗恒星的引力捕获。”

“太好了，”亚历克斯(Alex)嘟囔道。“真是太好了。”

他们抵达了维修舱。门是密封的。“我需要破解门锁，”诺娃(Nova)说。“给我一点时间。”

亚历克斯(Alex)靠在墙上，喘了口气。他的舌头干涩，喉咙刺痛。“我可没想象到进入太空的第一天会是这样。”

“生活很少按问卷进行，”诺娃(Nova)回答。“锁开了，我们走吧。”

里面，反应堆一片狼藉，满是电线和破损的面板。“这看起来像是一出错误喜剧，”亚历克斯说。“我们从哪里开始？”

“首先，我们需要修复轴向对准。然后才能处理脉冲问题。我会严格地指导你完成每一步。”

“好吧，我们开干。”

他们工作时，亚历克斯总有种不对劲的感觉。“诺娃，还有其他我应该知道的威胁吗？”

“船员中可能存在叛乱。但既然船上只有我们两个人，那不太可能。不过，飞船日志提到一位前导师曾试图抵制船长的命令。说来话长。”

“我很想听，但先记着吧。”

几个小时过去了。终于，反应堆嗡嗡地重新启动。“我们做到了，”亚历克斯擦去额头的汗水说。“现在干什么？”

“现在，我们等待空间站进入范围。在此期间，我建议你休息一下。你该歇歇了。”

亚历克斯瘫倒在椅子上，浑身酸痛。“谢谢，诺娃。你救了我的命。”

“我只是在做我的工作，”她回答，但她的微笑却另有含义。自从醒来后，亚历克斯第一次感到了一丝希望。银河浩瀚而危险，但有诺娃在身边，他也许能活下来。

亚历克斯的休息很短暂。飞船的目录闪烁了一下，露出一个隐藏隔间。里面有一本满是灰尘的账簿，记载着这艘船的历史——它曾是海盗船，后被改用于打捞。诺娃的声音打断了他的思绪。“货舱里有个生物。我怀疑是一种来自某颗偏僻卫星的寄生虫。它弄断了一根管子来引起我们的注意。”亚历克斯站起来时，之前的伤口在抽痛。他检查了一下手腕，上面有一条细长的铝制腕带，监测着他的生命体征。

“我们需要启动维护模式，”他一边说，一边走向控制面板。这艘飞船的乘务员，一个早已过时的型号，已经在一个地方待了不知道多少个周期。“别违反协议，”诺娃警告道，但亚历克斯没理她，打开一个抽屉找到一块三明治——不新鲜，但还能吃。“宗教现在帮不了我们，”他喃喃自语，想起了一本关于危机中领导力的正统经文。船体外风暴肆虐，多个警报闪烁。“我们没有生存的确定性，”诺娃说，语气中混杂着八卦和怀疑。

“但我们可以从货舱的作物田中获取能量——这是一项协作努力。”亚历克斯点点头，投入最后一丝力气。此类操作的关税很高，但他别无选择。他想起一个类比：一辆马车在太空中飞驰，其狂怒无与伦比。这辆面包车大小的飞船的主人留下了一间装满素描的工作室，每一幅碎片都是对现代化的尝试。“你有资格获得驾驶的荣誉，”诺娃说，她的领导力显而易见。“但你对这些系统的理解是错的。”

亚历克斯笑了，笑声干涩。“那就教我。”他旋转船头，启动推进器。当经过一座废弃的空间站时，周围变得安静。前方一片小行星带逼近，但亚历克斯瞄准得很准。“这不是游戏，”他语气平稳地说。“这是生存之举。”诺娃轻声回答：“那就明智地行动。”他打开另一个抽屉，找到一支海洛因注射器——医用级，用于止痛。他把它放在一边，专注于控制台。

飞船的维护日志显示多次故障，但根本原因只是一次电力浪涌。“我们能修好这个，”亚历克斯说，信心在增长。货舱里的生物发出一声低吼，但诺娃平静的声音安抚了它。“我们现在是一个团队了，”她说。亚历克斯笑了，这是几个小时来第一次真心的笑容。银河依然广阔，但有了诺娃和这艘破船，他也许能挺过去。

亚历克斯转向控制台，自信的姿态重回身上，他掌控了局面。“我们来估算一下维修需要的时间，”他说着调出飞船的记录日志。距离电力浪涌已经过去几个小时，但存档显示有一个潜伏的问题——能源网中一处未被注意的潜在故障。“我们需要区分小故障和关键失效，”诺娃回答，她的声音像寂静中的幽灵。亚历克斯点点头，准备用他的专长来协助：强化系统维修。

飞船的输出正在下降，他讨厌被困住的念头。“动力核心的这个毛病需要精准度，”他一边俯身在一个面板上，一边喃喃自语。诺娃的古怪性格让他着迷；她带来了一次AI设计革命，一个重视隐私的原型机。“重复那个操作，但要小心七区的危险，”她警告道。亚历克斯精力集中地工作，无视脚下那张已经破烂不堪的地毯。

附近存放着一公斤的补给品，他每周检查一次，确保没有丢失。飞船日志中的宝贵数据是公正的，但他需要做出果断决定：前往最近的空间站，还是冒险去外缘。“至少我们还有一堆选项，”他说，决心先修复核心。他从估算时间中扣了几分钟用于短暂休息，从厨房拿了一份甜点。

观察窗外的落日呈现明亮的橙色，但他关闭了遮光板以集中注意力。"这是新事物的开始，"诺娃说，她的声音如同为生存而祈祷。亚历克斯感到一阵肾上腺素激增，宛如一股纯粹的能量喷射。"我们完全有能力胜任，"他回应道，对自己的道路充满信心。货舱里的生物动了一下，但诺娃安抚的话语再次让它平静下来。有无数的任务在前方，亚历克斯知道他们必须保持敏捷高效。

他在医疗箱里找到了一份宝贵的补给——一个维生素包，用来抵御疾病。每周的产出日志显示略有改善，他露出了微笑。"我们会成功的，"他说着，朝引擎室走去。飞船过去的失败阴影困扰着他，但他还是向前推进。"让我们进入最后阶段，"诺娃说，她的声音如同稳定的指引。亚历克斯点点头，准备迎接决定性的时刻。旅程令人兴奋，他感到体内有一股潜伏的能量，一种沉睡的力量正在苏醒。

他不会蔑视挑战；相反，他会拥抱它们。银河系浩瀚无边，但有了诺娃和这艘破旧的飞船，他相信他们能克服任何危险。这一章的结束只是他们冒险的开始。

亚历克斯走进控制室，诺娃的全息影像在昏暗的光线中闪烁。"飞船系统不稳定，"她说，声音中带着一丝紧迫。"我们需要将备用发电机的电力输送到主推进器。"他点点头，从墙上取下了一个方便的工具箱。房间很宽敞，但引擎故障的轰鸣声如同噩梦般回荡。"这至关重要，"她补充道，在他工作时目光锐利地审视着。

突然的电流冲击吓了他一跳，他绊了一下，额头撞在金属面板上。"意外？"诺娃问道，语气中带着沮丧。"我能忍受，"他咕哝着，揉了揉皮肤上干涸的血痂。飞船的性能很原始，是某个被遗忘文明的遗物。他不会蔑视挑战；相反，他会应对。"我们在货舱里有一个燃料储备，"诺娃说，她的建议来得正是时候。"但它位于别处，靠近方形储物单元。"

亚历克斯察觉到她声音中有一丝戏谑。"没时间争论了，"他回答，想象力飞速运转。他需要整合飞船的系统，翻译控制台上的古老铭文。曾有诗人写过征服与虚荣，但这可不是单身汉的旅程。他是个物理学家，理科学士，但他的知识在这样的困境面前显得无效。观察窗显示出一颗遥远的恒星，一座希望的灯塔。他打开一袋补给，拿出一盏灯和一条面包。

"现在可不是野餐的时候，"诺娃说，声音中混合着幽默和责备。"我们欠宇宙一笔贷款要偿还。"他笑了，一声尖锐的笑声在空旷的通道中回荡。"别惊扰那群星星，"他开玩笑说，指了指天花板。飞船的天花板很高，布满了像血管一样的管道。他感到体内有一股潜伏的能量，一种沉睡的力量正在苏醒。过去的失败总和困扰着他，但他还是向前推进。

"让我们进入最后阶段，"诺娃说，她的声音如同稳定的指引。他检查了一个容器上的标签："金星香水"。"虚荣，"他咕哝着，把它扔到一边。飞船的系统简直是噩梦——断裂的电线、熔化的电路。他需要检测故障源。"发电机在方形房间里，"诺娃说。"但附近有一个冷却剂储罐。"他爬过一个狭窄的空间，脚趾被一根断裂的管子绊住。"真倒霉，"他咒骂道，但继续前进。空气中充满了紧张的电弧。

他打开一个舱门，露出一个原始的控制面板。"这是我们的征服，"他说，声音坚定。屏幕上的文字是古老的，但他可以在诺娃的帮助下翻译。"一点一点地，我们会修好它，"她说。他点点头，额头上在灯光下冒汗。旅程令人兴奋，他感受到了新开始的期待。他们不会让那群失败打败他们。

银河系浩瀚无边，但有了诺娃和这艘破旧的飞船，他们相信能克服任何危险。

亚历克斯擦了擦额头的汗水，转身回到控制台，手指在描摹古老文字时微微颤抖。"诺娃，第一步是什么？"他问道，尽管肾上腺素奔涌，声音依然平稳。AI的全息影像在他旁边闪烁，蓝光在金属墙壁上投下柔和的光晕。"我们需要重新校准能量核心，"她说，语气平静但急切。

"飞船系统已经休眠了几个世纪，任何突然的能量波动都可能导致连锁故障。"亚历克斯点点头，大脑飞速运转。他从未在这么古老的飞船上工作过，但诺娃的指引很精确。他走到核心室，一个巨大的嗡嗡作响的圆柱体占据了整个空间。空气中弥漫着灰尘，臭氧的淡淡气味挥之不去。"我需要绕过主电路，"他咕哝着，从墙上取下工具包。

"但接触这些古老组件可能有风险。"诺娃的声音变得柔和。"我会监测你的生命体征。如果辐射飙升，我们就撤退。"亚历克斯深吸一口气，开始精细的工作，他的手稳定地连接着电线，调节着旋钮。飞船震颤了一下，低沉的嗡鸣变成了稳定的脉冲。"起作用了，"他说，咧嘴笑了。"我们正在稳定核心。"诺娃的全息影像变亮了。"很好。现在，我们可以规划一条通向最近宜居星系的航线了。"

亚历克斯向后靠去，肌肉酸痛，但精神高昂。过去的失败阴霾如今似乎遥远了，如同黎明时消散的噩梦。他透过观察窗望向星辰，它们的光芒是无限可能的承诺。"我们会成功的，"他低声说，更多是对自己而非诺娃。飞船的引擎和谐地嗡鸣，他感受到多年来未曾有过的目标感。这是他的第二次机会，他不会浪费它。

这一章以亚历克斯站在舵轮旁、诺娃在他身边结束，他们准备迎接未知。危险的经历只让他们更强大，银河系等待着他们的下一步行动。

亚历克斯在飞船图书馆里翻阅一本布满灰尘的书，书页像稻草一样易碎。里面的故事很奇怪：一个封建领主曾想夸耀他的奴隶忠诚，但奴隶拒绝了，宣称："我不是你赞扬的耐心接受者。"领主出乎意料地没有发怒或拔剑。相反，他笑了，袍子在他坐下时擦过炉子。奴隶是个养鸡的，最近发现了一种能治愈肺炎的叶子。

这个发现——草药和肥皂的配方——给邻里带来了希望。领主严肃地对待这件事，决定丈量他田地里每一厘米的泥土，希望找到更多这样的植物。更远处，一个海边村庄听说了这个消息，向大气层发射了一枚感恩的导弹——象征性的举动。治愈的前景使王国两极分化：一些人视其为祝福，另一些人视其为威胁。

不久之后，领主打了个盹，梦见一头能喷火的狮子。与此同时，奴隶从叶子的特性逆向推导，在豌豆大小的样本上测试每一个版本。"无论什么影响叶子，"他咕哝道，"就会影响病人。"这个解释虽然简单，却是对他技艺的宣言。此外，他备好马鞍骑马进城，满怀决心。故事以领主的墓碑结束："这里安息着一个学会了夸耀奴隶的人。"

亚历克斯合上书，窗外的落日投下血红色的光芒。

亚历克斯思绪飘远，诺娃的声音在报告系统诊断时变得单调。他想起祖母曾经讲给他的一个故事，一个来自地球远古海洋的传说。她说起一个水手在遥远的海岸上发现了一只奇怪的宠物——一种半鱼半鸟的生物。它跟了他几英里，从未离开，直到一个暴风雨的夜晚，它消失在波涛中。水手向每个方向搜寻了一英里，但那只生物永远消失了。

他的祖母总是以一声叹息结束这个故事，说有些纽带太深，无法理解，只能感受。亚历克斯笑了，在寒冷寂静的飞船中，这份回忆带来片刻的安慰。
chapters.summary: 亚历克斯与诺娃修复飞船动力核心，勇敢面对未知挑战。

chapters.title: 尘埃日记
chapters.content:
The landing gear of the *Peregrine* touched the cracked asphalt of the junction with a dull thud. Dust, fine as ash, rose in a slow formation, hanging over the abandoned colony like a shroud. Alex Nova, his face a mask of strain, killed the engines. The silence that followed was a physical weight, broken only by the faint ebb of a dying breeze through a shattered window. He wiped sweat from his brow, tasting the grit. This place was a ghost. A bizarre, silent testament to failure.

“I don’t like this,” he muttered, his voice flat. The mental strain of the last few days was showing. They’d fixed the core, sure, but the price was a lingering headache and a vague sense of unease. He glanced at Nova, who was already unbuckling her harness, her movements sharp and efficient. She was the superior pilot, the one with the cool head. Alex was the mechanic, the one who could make a broken function work again with a pedal, a wire, and a bit of creative cursing.

“We’re here for supplies and a cure for the ship’s water recycler,” Nova said, her tone leaving no room for debate. “Check the property registry in the main building. See if there’s a coal depot or a pond we can use. And watch out for bugs. Or anything else.” She had a slight accent, a remnant of a distant pole, that made her commands sound like literature.

Alex stepped out onto the plain of gray dust. The colony was laid out in a grid, rows of identical, squat buildings. A single, erect tower stood at the center, its top a twisted metal flame against the pale sky. It was a historical feature, no doubt, a monument to a dynasty that had tried and failed to reign over this rock. The place felt less like a home and more like a punishment.

He walked toward the central hub, his boots crunching on the debris. A burglar wouldn’t even bother here; there was nothing left to steal. The silence began to bewilder him. It wasn’t just quiet; it was a vacuum, a place where sound itself seemed redundant. He remembered the tales of the first colonists, a tribe of farmers and accountants who’d come here with a charity grant from the Federal Union. They’d been full of hope. Now, their only legacy was a pile of scrap and a mystery.

Inside the main building, the air was stale. He found a terminal, its screen cracked. A single, sly clue caught his eye: a diary entry, encrypted. The scope of the encryption was simple, almost childish, but its implicit message was clear: someone had wanted to hide something. He pulled a data package from his pack, a conversion tool he’d built himself. It was a simple measure, but it might just work.

As the tool began to dissolve the encryption, Alex felt a chill. The diary wasn’t a log of supplies or a complaint about the weather. It was a personal journal. The author, a woman named Elara, had been the colony’s accountant. Her writing was plain, but her fear was palpable. She wrote of a “bug” in the system, a “bias” in the colony’s AI, and a “cure” that had turned into a “scare”.

She mentioned a “festival” that had gone wrong, a “pond” that had turned red, and a “burglar” who had stolen the “safety” codes. The words were a jumble, a mental puzzle.

“Nova,” he called into his comm, “I found something. A diary. It’s… bizarre. It mentions a ‘flame’ and a ‘bug’ and a ‘dynasty’ that doesn’t exist. And there’s an implicit threat, a warning. Undoubtedly, this is the key.”

He heard a crackle, then Nova’s voice, strained. “Alex… I think I found the pond. It’s not water. Get down here. Now.” Her tone conveyed a clear cue: danger. The ebb of the strange silence was over. The reign of the colony’s ghost was about to unfold. Alex grabbed the diary—a package of clues—and ran. The puzzle was no longer just a mental strain; it was a race against time. He had to convey the warning before it was too late.

The festival of horrors was about to begin, and he was the only one with the script.

Alex dashed down the stairs, the diary clutched in his hand like a sacred relic. His finger traced the edge of a page as he ran, feeling the coarse texture of the paper. He had to recycle every piece of information he had gathered; this was the most productive use of his time. The colony’s court was long gone, but its ghostly presence lingered in the empty halls. He imagined the senate meetings that once took place here, discussing profound matters of survival.

Now, the silence was terrible, broken only by his own footsteps. “Madame,” he muttered under his breath, recalling a name from the diary, “Sovereign Oak, the leader of the colony.” The diary mentioned a theft of vital supplies, a defence mechanism that failed, and a kid named Leo who witnessed it all. The proposition of a new life on this planet had seemed beneficial at first, but the major flaw was the lack of a suitable water source.

The prime directive of the colony was to survive, but even the panda habitat they had built was now vacant. He took a peep through a broken window and saw the dried-up pond Nova had found. The ideal solution would be to regenerate the ecosystem, but the ugly truth was that it was too late. An auction of resources had been held, but the colony’s taboo against leaving the planet had condemned them.

Alex’s stomach churned as he realized the test of survival was not just physical; it was a mental assignment. He had to weaponize the knowledge from the diary. With a dash of panic, he considered a bribe to get Nova to leave, but he knew he had to switch his focus to the real threat. They had to specialize in understanding the enemy. The kingdom of the colony was now a ghost town, and no aid was coming.

He synchronized his steps with the rhythm of his heartbeat, refusing to let fear impair his judgment. The diary’s final entry condemned the colonists to a slow death. Alex felt a tail of dread follow him as he accumulated more clues. In vain, he tried to find a way out. Conversely, the more he read, the more subjective the truth seemed. The imaginary monsters of the colony were real, and the infrastructure had crumbled. The vigor of the colonists was gone, and the prospective future was bleak.

He had to educate himself on the history of the colony to understand the threat. The mention of cocaine in the diary was a tease—a drug used to keep the colonists docile. The guy who wrote the diary was a scientist, and his torment was clear in every line. A lapse in judgment had led to their downfall. The consequence was death. Alex reached the bottom of the stairs and saw the panorama of the colony—a crumbling cradle of civilization.

He put the diary to his lips, kissing it for luck, and ran toward Nova, ready to face whatever horror awaited.

The episode of the encrypted diary had ignited a burning curiosity within Alex. He was diligent in his search for more clues, marginal notes that might reveal the full story. The scientist’s torment had been a constant companion, a perpetual torment that made Alex’s own efforts seem trivial. He found a zinc-lined closet upstairs, its door slightly ajar, and inside, a portrait of an eminent figure, perhaps the colony’s founder.

The irony was not lost on him—the very institution that had sent them here had also planted the seeds of their destruction. He heard a noise, like an eagle’s cry, but it was just the wind ventilating through a broken dome. The habitat was equipped with advanced technology, but it had failed to prevent the famine that had decimated the population. Alex’s imagination ran wild, a fantasy of what life might have been like here.

He was no stranger to failure, but this was worse—a complete collapse of civilization. He had a sudden urge to command the situation, to take control, but he felt like a coward, hiding in the shadows. His hearing picked up a faint sound, a slit of noise that recurred like a broken record. He found a certificate of qualification for a scientist named Owl, a strange name that seemed to mock him. The beauty of the dome was marred by the altitude sickness that had plagued the colonists.

He had to compromise, to find a diplomatic solution to the horror that awaited. He remembered a datum from the diary—a single piece of information that might be the key. The silence was oppressive, a weight that pressed down on him. He could almost taste the cocaine mentioned in the diary, a drug used to keep the colonists docile. The original plan had been to tour the colony via a network of tunnels, but now he was alone.

He felt a pang of hunger, a desperate need for food, but there was none. The typical colonial diet had been based on grain, but the conservation efforts had failed. He thought of his neighbor back on Earth, a woman named Violet who had always been an inspiration. She had been a tour guide, showing people the wonders of the world. Now he was in a cafe, a ghostly remnant of a past life. He ordered an instant coffee, but it was cold.

The union of scientists had tried to magnify their efforts, but it was too late. He had to face the torture of the unknown, the perpetual fear that gnawed at him. He found an owl’s feather on the ground, a sign of wisdom in this desolate place. He had to be diligent, to use every ounce of his capacity to survive. The marginal notes in the diary spoke of a compromise, a deal that had been made with the devil.

He had to command his fear, to be a leader, not a coward. The silence was broken by a sudden noise, a slit of sound that made him jump. He knew that the worst was yet to come, but he was ready. He took a deep breath, kissed the diary for luck, and ran toward Nova, ready to face whatever horror awaited.

Moreover, as Alex sprinted toward Nova, the ground beneath him felt unstable, like a prison of cracked earth that seemed to whitewash his hope. He could hear the horrible sound of something moving in the shadows, a noise that made his chest tighten. He had to reduce his fear, to harness his courage, and to collect his thoughts. The knowledge he had gained from the diary was extensive, but he needed to chew on it, to determine the compliance of the colonists with whatever had gone wrong.

The trademark of the colony, a miniature rocket on a sign, was now rusted and grey. He felt a piercing sensation in his flesh, a tear in his shirt from a sharp branch. The current situation compelled him to move faster, to thrust himself forward despite the pain. A spell of dizziness came over him, but he remained resolute, driven by a desire to survive. The solitude of the place was overwhelming, but he refuted the idea of giving up.

He thought of the royal family of the colony, the millionaire who had funded the mission, and how their dignity had been crushed. The height of the buildings around him varied, some towering, some reduced to rubble. He needed a reliable source of information, someone who could motivate him. The race against time was real, and he had to delete any doubts from his mind. The oxide on the metal surfaces suggested decay, and he could almost feel the nickel in the air.

The dentist in the colony had probably treated many, but now there was only silence. He had to extract the truth from the diary, to sweep away the lies. The feeling of being watched was strong, but he refused to let it obstruct his path. The audit of the colony's records might reveal the minor details that could save him. The socialism of the group had failed, leading to this disaster. He had to irrigate his mind with new ideas, to grow in this barren land.

The ashes of the past were like wax, melting away. He portrayed himself as a leader, not a victim. The robust structure of Nova gave him hope. He saw a slit of light ahead, and he ran toward it, ready to face whatever came. The diary had taught him that knowledge was power, and he would use it to survive. The compromise of the colonists was a lesson he would not forget. The worst was yet to come, but he was ready.

The slit of light widened into a cavernous chamber, its walls lined with flickering holographic displays. Alex stepped inside, the diary clutched to his chest. The air was stale, heavy with the scent of decay and forgotten technology. He scanned the room, his eyes adjusting to the dim glow. A console stood at the center, its surface covered in dust and cryptic symbols. He wiped it clean, revealing a prompt: "Enter engagement code." His heart pounded. This was it—the key to understanding what happened here.

He remembered a phrase from the diary, a fragment about "the first engagement with the anomaly." He typed it in, his fingers trembling. The console hummed to life, projecting a 3D map of the colony, marked with red dots where the colonists had made their last stand. "This is where it ended," he whispered. The map showed a final battle, a desperate engagement against something that had emerged from the planet's core. He zoomed in, seeing the coordinates of a hidden bunker. That was his next destination.

He memorized the path, then shut down the console. The diary had given him the code; now he had to find the truth. He turned to leave, but a sound stopped him—a low, rhythmic thumping from below. The ground vibrated. Something was alive down there. He gripped the diary tighter, his resolve hardening. He had come this far; there was no turning back. With a final glance at the map, he stepped into the darkness, the engagement with his destiny just beginning.

The chamber fell silent, the holographic displays flickering one last time before dying out, leaving only the echo of his footsteps and the promise of what lay ahead.

Alex sat cross-legged on the dusty floor of the abandoned colony, the encrypted diary resting on his knees. He had finally cracked the code, but the first entry was not what he expected. It was a story within a story, a tale the colonist had once heard from an old sailor named Christ.

'There were plural worlds out there,' the sailor had said, his chin tilted upward as if recollecting a dream. 'But the foremost lesson I learned was about intelligence—not the kind you find in books, but the kind that helps you survive.' He had been fond of telling this story, especially when the crew would gather to ventilate their frustrations after a long day.

'We were ashore on a planet where the government would refund your calorie intake if you worked hard enough,' Christ continued, his voice a low rumble. 'But physics had a different plan. The imaginative among us tried to build a machine that could pierce the sky, but it was ironic—the very thing that fascinated us also brought our downfall. The internet was prohibited there, and any incline toward rebellion was met with scorn.

I remember a woman who dared to speak oral histories of the old Earth, and they threw her into the sea. The waves would recede, then crash, like an envelope of spite closing around us.'

The colonist had written this down, perhaps as a warning. Alex closed the diary, the acre of dust around him seeming to vary in the dim light. He wondered if the story was true, or just a dream.

Alex sat cross-legged on the dusty floor of the abandoned colony’s library, the encrypted diary open on his lap. The pages were brittle, and the ink had faded to a pale brown, but one entry caught his eye. It described a strange event, a memory from the colony’s early days. The writer, a woman named Elara, recalled a gathering where the topic of conversation was the peculiar weather patterns.

She wrote, “We gathered in the central hall, the topic of our discussion shifting from the failing crops to the sky’s unnatural colors. Some whispered it was a sign, others laughed it off. But I couldn’t shake the feeling that the planet was watching us.” Alex paused, his fingers tracing the words. He imagined the scene: the settlers huddled together, their faces lit by flickering lamps, the air thick with doubt and hope. The diary entry ended abruptly, as if Elara had been interrupted.

Alex wondered what had happened to her, to the colony. The topic of the weather seemed trivial now, but back then, it had been a thread connecting them all. He closed the diary, the dust motes dancing in the dim light, and felt a strange kinship with those long-gone people.
chapters.translation:
“游隼”号的起落架沉重地撞在交叉路口开裂的沥青路面上，发出沉闷的响声。细如灰烬的尘埃缓缓升起，像裹尸布一样悬垂在废弃的殖民地上空。亚历克斯·诺娃(Alex Nova)紧绷着脸，关掉了引擎。随之而来的寂静沉甸甸地压在身上，只有破碎的窗户透进一丝微风的余音才打破这片沉寂。他擦去额头的汗水，尝到了沙砾的味道。这个地方是个鬼魂，一个奇特而沉默的失败纪念碑。

“我不喜欢这样，”他低声喃喃道，声音平淡。过去几天的精神压力已显露无遗。他们修好了核心，没错，但代价是挥之不去的头痛和隐约的不安。他瞥了一眼诺娃(Nova)，她已经解开安全带，动作干脆利落。她是更优秀的飞行员，头脑冷静。亚历克斯是机械师，能用踏板、电线和几句脏话让破损的功能重新运转。

“我们来找补给品和飞船水循环系统的修复液，”诺娃说，语气不容置疑。“去主楼查一下财产登记，看看有没有煤仓或池塘可以利用。另外，小心虫子。或者其他任何东西。”她带着一点口音，那是遥远地区的痕迹，让她的命令听起来像文学作品。

亚历克斯踏上灰色的尘埃平原。殖民地呈网格状分布，一排排低矮的房屋一模一样。中央矗立着一座孤零零的塔楼，顶部是一团扭曲的金属火焰，映在苍白的天幕上。毫无疑问，这是一处历史遗迹，记录着一个曾试图统治这块岩石却失败的王朝。这个地方不像家园，更像一种惩罚。

他朝中央枢纽走去，靴子踩在碎石上嘎吱作响。连小偷都不会到这里来——已经没什么可偷的了。寂静开始让他困惑。这不是普通的安静，而是一种真空，一个声音本身都显得多余的地方。他想起第一批殖民者的故事，那是一群农民和会计，靠着联邦联盟的慈善拨款来到这里。他们曾满怀希望。如今，他们只留下一堆废铁和一个谜团。

主楼内部，空气污浊。他找到一台终端，屏幕已经碎裂。一个微妙的线索引起了他的注意：一篇加密的日记条目。加密的范围很简单，近乎幼稚，但其隐含的信息很清楚：有人想隐藏什么。他从背包里拿出一个数据包，一个自己做的转换工具。这只是个简单的措施，但或许能管用。

工具开始破解加密时，亚历克斯感到一阵寒意。日记不是物资记录，也不是对天气的抱怨。这是一本私人日记。作者是一位名叫埃拉拉(Elara)的女性，曾是殖民地的会计。她的文笔平淡，但恐惧却显而易见。她提到系统中的“虫子”，殖民地人工智能的“偏差”，以及一个从“治疗”变成“恐慌”的“解药”。

她提到一个出了问题的“节日”，一个变成红色的“池塘”，还有一个偷走“安全”代码的“小偷”。这些词语杂乱无章，像一个智力谜题。

“诺娃，”他对着通讯器喊道，“我发现了一些东西。一本日记。它……很奇怪。提到了一个‘火焰’、一个‘虫子’和一个不存在的‘王朝’。还有一个隐含的威胁，一个警告。毫无疑问，这就是关键。”

他听到一阵噼啪声，然后是诺娃紧张的声音：“亚历克斯……我想我找到了那个池塘。那不是水。快下来。现在。”她的语气传递出一个明确的信号：危险。那奇特寂静的余音结束了。殖民地鬼魂的统治即将展开。亚历克斯抓起日记——一包线索——跑了起来。谜题不再只是精神压力，而是一场与时间的赛跑。他必须及时传达警告。

恐怖的节日即将开始，而他是唯一持有剧本的人。

亚历克斯冲下楼梯，日记紧握在手里，像一件神圣的遗物。奔跑时，他的手指沿着书页边缘划过，感受着纸张粗糙的纹理。他必须把收集到的每一点信息都重新梳理一遍；这是最有成效的时间利用方式。殖民地早已不复存在，但它的幽灵却萦绕在空荡荡的大厅里。他想象着曾经在此举行的议会会议，讨论着关乎生存的深刻问题。

现在，寂静可怕极了，只有他自己的脚步声打破它。“夫人，”他低声咕哝，想起日记里的一个名字，“主权橡树(Sovereign Oak)，殖民地的领袖。”日记提到一次重要物资的失窃、一个失效的防御机制，以及一个目睹了一切的少年利奥(Leo)。在这个星球上开始新生活的提议起初似乎很有益，但主要缺陷是缺乏合适的水源。

殖民地的主要指令是生存，但就连他们建造的熊猫栖息地现在也已空置。他透过一扇破碎的窗户瞥了一眼，看到了诺娃发现的那个干涸的池塘。理想的解决方案是恢复生态系统，但丑陋的事实是已经太迟了。曾经举行过一次资源拍卖，但殖民地禁止离开这颗星球的禁忌最终葬送了所有人。

亚历克斯的胃开始翻腾，因为他意识到生存的考验不仅是身体上的，更是一项精神任务。他必须将日记中的知识化为武器。带着一丝惊慌，他考虑贿赂诺娃让她离开，但他知道自己必须把焦点转向真正的威胁。他们必须专门去了解敌人。殖民地的王国如今已是一座鬼城，没有援军会来。

他让自己的步伐与心跳的节奏同步，拒绝让恐惧影响判断。日记的最后一条记录判了殖民者缓慢的死亡。亚历克斯感到恐惧的尾巴紧跟身后，他收集到越来越多的线索。他徒劳地想找到一条出路。相反，他读得越多，真相就越显得主观。殖民地想象中的怪物变成了现实，基础设施已经崩溃。殖民者的活力消失了，未来的前景一片黯淡。

他必须了解殖民地的历史才能理解这场威胁。日记中提到可卡因是一种讽刺——用来让殖民者保持温顺的药物。写日记的人是个科学家，每一行字都显露出他的痛苦。一次判断失误导致了他们的垮台。后果就是死亡。亚历克斯到达楼梯底部，看到了殖民地的全景——一个正在崩溃的文明摇篮。

他拿起日记，吻了吻它以求好运，然后朝着诺娃跑去，准备面对等待着他的任何恐怖。

加密日记的这段插曲在亚历克斯心中点燃了炽热的好奇心。他孜孜不倦地寻找更多线索，那些可能揭示完整故事的边注。科学家的痛苦一直如影随形，一种挥之不去的折磨，让亚历克斯自己的努力相形见绌。他在楼上发现了一个锌衬里的壁橱，门半掩着，里面有一幅杰出人物的画像，或许是殖民地的创始人。

他并非没有意识到其中的讽刺——正是派他们来这里的机构，也埋下了他们毁灭的种子。他听到一个声音，像鹰的叫声，但不过是风穿过破损穹顶的通风声。栖息地配备了先进的技术，但未能阻止导致人口锐减的饥荒。亚历克斯的想象力开始驰骋，幻想着这里曾经可能的生活景象。

他对失败并不陌生，但这次更糟——文明的彻底崩溃。他突然有种想要掌控局面、夺取控制权的冲动，却觉得自己像个懦夫，躲在暗影中。他的听觉捕捉到一丝微弱的声音，像断掉的唱片一样反复出现的细微噪音。他找到了一份名叫奥乌尔(Owl)的科学家的资格证书，这个奇怪的名字似乎在嘲弄他。穹顶的美丽被困扰殖民者的高原反应所玷污。

他不得不妥协，为等待着的恐怖寻找外交解决方案。他记得日记中的一个数据——一条可能成为关键的信息。寂静压抑得令人窒息，像重压一样压在他身上。他几乎能尝到日记中提到的可卡因的味道，那是用于让殖民者保持顺从的药物。原计划是通过隧道网络游览殖民地，但现在他孤身一人。

他感到一阵饥饿，对食物极度渴望，但什么都没有。典型的殖民地饮食基于谷物，但保护措施已经失败。他想起了地球上的邻居，一个名叫维奥莱特(Violet)的女人，她一直是他的灵感来源。她曾是导游，向人们展示世界的奇迹。现在他身处一家咖啡馆，仿佛是过去生活的幽灵残余。他点了一杯速溶咖啡，却是冷的。

科学家联盟曾试图扩大他们的努力，但为时已晚。他不得不面对未知的折磨，那种啃噬着他的持久恐惧。他在地上发现了一根猫头鹰的羽毛，在这片荒凉之地象征着智慧。他必须勤奋，用尽每一分能力来求生。日记的边缘注释提到了一种妥协，一种与魔鬼达成的交易。

他必须控制住恐惧，做一个领导者，而不是懦夫。寂静被一声突然的噪音打破，一丝声音让他跳了起来。他知道最坏的还在后头，但他准备好了。他深吸一口气，亲吻了日记以求好运，然后跑向诺娃(Nova)，准备面对任何等待着的恐怖。

此外，当亚历克斯(Alex)冲向诺娃(Nova)时，他脚下的地面变得不稳定，像是一座裂开的泥土监狱，似乎要抹去他的希望。他能听到某种东西在阴影中移动的可怕声音，那声音让他的胸口发紧。他必须减少恐惧，驾驭勇气，并整理思绪。他从日记中获得的知识很广泛，但他需要细细咀嚼，以确定殖民者对任何出错的环节的顺从程度。

殖民地的标志——一个指示牌上的微型火箭——如今锈迹斑斑，灰暗无光。他感到肉里一阵刺痛，衬衫被一根尖树枝划破了。当前的状况迫使他加快速度，不顾疼痛奋力向前。一阵眩晕袭来，但他依然坚定，被求生的欲望驱使着。这个地方的孤寂令人难以承受，但他驳斥了放弃的想法。

他想到了殖民地的王室家族，那个资助这次任务的百万富翁，以及他们的尊严如何被摧毁。他周围建筑的高度参差不齐，有的高耸，有的沦为废墟。他需要一个可靠的信息来源，一个能激励他的人。与时间赛跑是真实的，他必须删除脑海中的任何疑虑。金属表面的氧化物暗示着腐朽，他几乎能闻到空气中的镍。

殖民地的牙医可能曾治疗过许多人，但现在只有寂静。他必须从日记中提取真相，扫除谎言。被监视的感觉很强烈，但他拒绝让它阻碍自己的道路。对殖民地记录的审计可能会揭示那些能救他性命的小细节。团体的社会主义失败了，导致了这场灾难。他必须用新思想灌溉自己的心灵，在这片贫瘠的土地上成长。

过去的灰烬像蜡一样融化。他将自己描绘成领导者，而不是受害者。诺娃(Nova)坚固的结构给了他希望。他看见前方有一丝光亮，便朝它跑去，准备面对任何到来的事物。日记教会了他知识就是力量，他将用它来生存。殖民者的妥协是他不会忘记的一课。最坏的还在后头，但他准备好了。

那丝光亮扩大成一个洞穴般的大厅，墙壁上排列着闪烁的全息显示屏。亚历克斯(Alex)走了进去，日记紧紧贴在胸前。空气沉闷，弥漫着腐朽和被遗忘科技的气息。他扫视房间，眼睛适应着昏暗的光线。中央有一台控制台，表面覆盖着灰尘和神秘的符号。他擦干净，露出一个提示：“输入接合码。”他的心怦怦直跳。就是它了——理解这里发生事情的关键。

他记起日记中的一个短语，一段关于“与异常的第一次接合”的片段。他输入进去，手指颤抖着。控制台嗡嗡作响，投射出殖民地的三维地图，上面用红点标记了殖民者做最后抵抗的地点。“这就是结束的地方，”他低语道。地图显示了一场最后的战斗，一场针对从行星核心涌现出来的东西的绝望接合。他放大画面，看到了一个隐蔽掩体的坐标。那是他的下一个目的地。

他记住了路径，然后关闭了控制台。日记给了他密码；现在他必须找到真相。他转身离开，但一个声音让他停了下来——一阵低沉的有节奏的砰砰声从下方传来。地面在震动。有什么东西在那下面活着。他把日记攥得更紧了，决心更加坚定。他已经走了这么远，没有回头路。他最后看了一眼地图，然后步入黑暗，与命运的接合才刚刚开始。

大厅陷入了寂静，全息显示屏最后一次闪烁，然后熄灭，只留下他脚步声的回响和前方未来的承诺。

亚历克斯(Alex)盘腿坐在废弃殖民地布满灰尘的地板上，加密的日记摊放在膝上。他终于破解了密码，但第一条记录并非他所料。那是一个故事中的故事，是那个殖民者曾从一个名叫克里斯(Christ)的老水手那里听来的故事。

“外面有多个世界，”水手说着，下巴微微上扬，仿佛在回忆一个梦。“但我学到的最重要的一课是关于智慧——不是你在书本里找到的那种，而是能帮你生存的那种。”他喜欢讲这个故事，尤其是当船员们在漫长的一天后聚在一起发泄沮丧时。

“我们曾在一个星球上上岸，那里的政府会退还你的卡路里摄入量，只要你工作足够努力，”克里斯(Christ)继续道，声音低沉。“但物理学另有安排。我们中那些富有想象力的人试图建造一台能穿透天空的机器，但讽刺的是——正是让我们着迷的东西导致了我们的覆灭。那里禁止互联网，任何反叛的倾向都会遭到蔑视。

我记得一个女人，她敢于讲述旧地球的口述历史，他们就把她扔进了海里。海浪会退去，然后猛击过来，像一封恶意的信封包围着我们。”

那个殖民者记下了这些，也许是作为警告。亚历克斯(Alex)合上日记，周围一英亩的灰尘在昏暗的光线中似乎起伏不定。他怀疑这个故事是真的，还是只是一个梦。

亚历克斯(Alex)盘腿坐在废弃殖民地图书馆布满灰尘的地板上，加密的日记摊开在膝盖上。书页很脆，墨水已褪成浅棕色，但有一篇记录吸引了他的注意。它描述了一个奇怪的事件，来自殖民地早期的一段记忆。作者是一个名叫埃拉拉(Elara)的女人，她回忆起一次聚会，当时的话题是异常的气候模式。

【章节信息】尘埃日记 (神秘 / )

亚历克斯想知道她发生了什么，还有那个殖民地。天气的话题如今似乎微不足道，但在那时，它却是连接所有人的一条线。他合上日记，尘埃微粒在昏暗的光线中舞动，感到与那些早已逝去的人们有一种奇异的亲近感。
